idiom_name: RetryLayer::new(Policy) around a Service, with clone_request for replay
implementation_notes: In async Rust the retry policy is middleware around a Service: implement tower::retry::Policy<Req, Res, E> (retry() decides from the result whether to try again and clone_request() says how the request is reproduced) and wrap the service with RetryLayer - the layer owns the attempt loop, so callers keep using the service normally and the policy composes with timeout, rate-limit and load-shed layers from the same crate. tower also ships a backoff module for delay strategies and a budget module that caps how many retries a fleet performs over time, which is the sanctioned answer to retry storms. The trade-off is structural: the request type must be clonable or reconstructible and the operation must be expressed as a Service, which is natural in tonic or hyper stacks and heavy for a one-off call.
pitfalls: clone_request returns Option: a policy that cannot reproduce the request (a consumed body, a non-clonable type) silently stops retrying, so the request type must be designed for replay.
Policy::retry is called with the inner call's result and must not block: sleeping belongs in the returned future, not inside retry().
Layer order decides semantics: a retry layer outside a load-shedding or timeout layer multiplies attempts through the whole stack.
No retry budget is implied: without tower::retry::budget or a backoff strategy, N clients retrying in lockstep can still hammer a recovering dependency.

variants.name: backon Retryable combinator with ExponentialBuilder and a Sleeper
variants.implementation_notes: backon adds retry to any function returning a Result: fetch.retry(ExponentialBuilder::default()).sleep(tokio::time::sleep).when(|e| ...).notify(|err, dur| ...).await - the Retryable and BlockingRetryable traits build a Retry combinator over the future (or the blocking call), the BackoffBuilder decides the delay (ConstantBuilder, ExponentialBuilder, FibonacciBuilder, all supporting jitter) and the Sleeper decides how the wait happens (tokio, futures-timer, embassy for no_std, or std::thread::sleep). Because the policy is a value built at the call site, this is the natural form outside a Service stack - scripts, CLI tools, background workers - and the blocking variant covers synchronous code with the same policy vocabulary. It replaces the hand-written loop with a combinator, at the cost of a trait-based call chain that has to be read as a pipeline.
variants.code_sketch:
let content = fetch
    .retry(ExponentialBuilder::default().with_jitter())
    .when(|e| matches!(e, Error::Transient(_)))     // classify
    .notify(|err, dur| tracing::warn!(?err, ?dur, "retrying"))
    .await?;
pitfalls: A Sleeper must be chosen: with no sleeper feature enabled and no custom implementation the crate fails to compile with the 'PleaseEnableAFeatureOrProvideACustomSleeper' error.
Closures that capture mutable state cannot be retried directly (the FnMut borrow escapes the async block); RetryableWithContext exists to pass ownership through the attempts.
when() inspects only the error value, so classification needs an error type that carries the reason - a boxed dyn Error makes the predicate stringly-typed.
Each attempt re-runs the whole future, so work performed before the failure is repeated and the operation must be idempotent.
